<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:alibi" data-paper-title="Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-alibi-69e595a8" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-accc8fac0a859481">Why does ALiBi address training short and testing long?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aalibi">Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Position mechanisms fitted only to training lengths can fail at greater distances. ALiBi computes a distance penalty directly in logits. The positional rule extrapolates; long-context accuracy is empirical.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After training on 512 words, compute distances for word 800 without looking up a learned 800th position.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2108.12409-alibi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-accc8fac0a859481">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:alibi" data-paper-title="Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d919373883619f72">Without position vectors, how does ALiBi tell how far apart tokens are?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aalibi">Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It subtracts a distance-proportional bias from each head&#x27;s attention logits. Distant tokens need a stronger content match, and slopes vary by head. The rule extrapolates without a fixed-length table, but that does not guarantee arbitrary-length retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Equal content scores at distances 2 and 20 favor the closer token; a distant answer can still win with a stronger match.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2108.12409-alibi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d919373883619f72">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:alibi" data-paper-title="Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e857b141de1beae3">Where do linear bias and position embeddings act?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aalibi">Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Position embeddings modify token inputs before Q/K/V projections. ALiBi does not learn position vectors; it modifies per-head matching logits directly. These are distinct information paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same content vectors can have different logit penalties at different distances.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2108.12409-alibi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e857b141de1beae3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:alibi" data-paper-title="Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e0295b696e351666">Can ALiBi&#x27;s distance penalty replace causal masking?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aalibi">Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta AI</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Bias changes preferences among visible positions, while the mask excludes future ones. Broadcast each head&#x27;s slope and keep causality. Small local models do not establish the paper&#x27;s large-scale gain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Token 3 cannot read token 4 even though their distance is one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2108.12409-alibi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e0295b696e351666">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:autonomy-heads" data-paper-title="Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-autonomy-heads-2d7238b5" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-460838ff2d888e65">What does data-free omit in Autonomy-of-Heads?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aautonomy-heads">Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It uses frozen Q/K geometry rather than calibration examples and runtime gating to choose sparsity. This does not remove model pretraining or post-sparsification evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Assign head types from weights before deployment, then check actual answers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06849">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.06849-autonomy-heads/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-460838ff2d888e65">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:autonomy-heads" data-paper-title="Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d644b6b25fc1e45">How can Autonomy-of-Heads assign sparse patterns without calibration examples?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aautonomy-heads">Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It analyzes frozen Q/K projections and uses spectral effective rank to characterize potential matching geometry, separating retrieval-oriented from streaming heads. No sample-based calibration or runtime selector is needed, but real tasks must validate the pattern.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two heads with equal budgets can emphasize very different numbers of directions; assign patterns accordingly and test evidence retention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06849">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.06849-autonomy-heads/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d644b6b25fc1e45">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:autonomy-heads" data-paper-title="Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4985c216e974937b">How does weight-based head assignment differ from dynamic attention selection?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aautonomy-heads">Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Weight geometry gives stable assignments and avoids per-input selector work. Dynamic methods adapt to content but pay selection cost. Neither accuracy follows from calibration cost alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A fixed retrieval head always reads far away, while a dynamic gate may allocate different ranges for short and long prompts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06849">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.06849-autonomy-heads/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4985c216e974937b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:autonomy-heads" data-paper-title="Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3f4c233f05443042">Can singular values be used as probabilities directly for spectral entropy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aautonomy-heads">Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Normalize them into a distribution, or rescaling the matrix changes entropy&#x27;s meaning. Handle degenerate cases. Local mini-suite checks data flow, not checkpoint quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>[2,2] and [20,20] both normalize to [0.5,0.5].</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06849">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.06849-autonomy-heads/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3f4c233f05443042">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:conv-llm" data-paper-title="Convolution for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-conv-llm-13d560f4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0cd712f5033c9b5c">What information preference does Conv-LLM add to attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aconv-llm">Convolution for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei / Peking University / Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Global matching accesses distant tokens without inherently emphasizing local word combinations. Short convolution first enriches Q/K/V with local order, while attention handles global interaction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Aggregate nearby words in “not very good” before reading broader context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18413">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.18413-conv-llm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0cd712f5033c9b5c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:conv-llm" data-paper-title="Convolution for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ca1d3cdc7932365e">Why add three-tap convolution after Q/K/V despite having attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aconv-llm">Convolution for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei / Peking University / Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Attention selects history by content. Short depthwise residual convolution adds nearby ordered patterns to projected Q/K/V before attention, without replacing global interaction. Left padding preserves causality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Local context can combine negation with already seen neighboring words before matching faraway context, but cannot read an unseen word.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18413">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.18413-conv-llm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ca1d3cdc7932365e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:conv-llm" data-paper-title="Convolution for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-30e7fcb1185be4fa">How does depthwise QKV convolution differ from replacing attention with convolution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aconv-llm">Convolution for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei / Peking University / Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It enriches projections without removing global attention. Depthwise kernels do not fully mix channels, keeping overhead small, and attention still serves long-range access.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Combine three adjacent positions, then still read a name hundreds of words earlier.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18413">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.18413-conv-llm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-30e7fcb1185be4fa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:conv-llm" data-paper-title="Convolution for Large Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-779d00242b977804">How should QKV residual convolution handle padding, activation, and bypass?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aconv-llm">Convolution for Large Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei / Peking University / Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use causal left padding, add the convolution to projected Q/K/V, then run attention. Do not insert normalization or activation into this documented bypass.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Width three at t uses t, t−1, t−2, not symmetric future padding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18413">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.18413-conv-llm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-779d00242b977804">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:dart" data-paper-title="DART: Decoded Attention over Recurrent States for Efficient Long-Context Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-dart-ebf1e36e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-322681ae4ecfb82c">Why make recurrent state queryable rather than only use it as a final summary?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adart">DART: Decoded Attention over Recurrent States for Efficient Long-Context Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Continuous updates can erase old information. DART retains chunk contributions for targeted access, giving long-range dependencies an addressable path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Retrieve chapter one&#x27;s state to answer a name question after many chapters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.02032-dart/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-322681ae4ecfb82c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:dart" data-paper-title="DART: Decoded Attention over Recurrent States for Efficient Long-Context Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c3968b3b16484d2a">Why keep recurrent states from several chunks instead of one final DART state?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adart">DART: Decoded Attention over Recurrent States for Efficient Long-Context Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed-capacity recurrence can overwrite old facts. DART decodes chunk-state contributions into queryable K/V, attends to them from the current token, and fuses memory reads with Mamba. Addressability costs extra storage and retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A later chapter may overwrite an earlier author&#x27;s name; retrieve the first chunk instead of relying on the final state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.02032-dart/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c3968b3b16484d2a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:dart" data-paper-title="DART: Decoded Attention over Recurrent States for Efficient Long-Context Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-339f62d5ba0a3b95">How does DART state memory differ from storing all token KV?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adart">DART: Decoded Attention over Recurrent States for Efficient Long-Context Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It reads K/V decoded from compressed recurrent chunks, not original K/V for every token. This trades storage and access flexibility and can still lose detail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Retrieving a chunk representation need not reconstruct every word.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.02032-dart/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-339f62d5ba0a3b95">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:dart" data-paper-title="DART: Decoded Attention over Recurrent States for Efficient Long-Context Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d8a5db2ce8d1be02">Which path should DART&#x27;s gate g_t modulate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Adart">DART: Decoded Attention over Recurrent States for Efficient Long-Context Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mamba is the main output; add gated state-memory attention. Separate recurrent updates, state-to-K/V decoding, and query reads. Do not gate the entire sum.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Near-zero g_t suppresses memory reads while preserving Mamba.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02032">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.02032-dart/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d8a5db2ce8d1be02">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:frac-ssm" data-paper-title="Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-frac-ssm-9d35422b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-88fb5b322da73fee">How does power-law memory differ from a recent window?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afrac-ssm">Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab, Montreal Research Center</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Old influence fades gradually instead of becoming zero at a fixed boundary. Frac-SSM approximates this with finite exponential modes at several timescales.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A past event can still matter weakly beyond the latest 100 steps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36314">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.36314-frac-ssm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-88fb5b322da73fee">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:frac-ssm" data-paper-title="Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-70c0b6310e5e85f1">How do finitely many recurrent states approximate long fractional-order power-law memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afrac-ssm">Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab, Montreal Research Center</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One exponential has one decay timescale. Log-spaced modes approximate a power-law tail: fast modes handle recent changes and slow ones keep older influence. Finite capacity and approximation range do not give unlimited exact memory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Fast, medium, and slow channels combine into a longer tail than one decay.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36314">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.36314-frac-ssm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-70c0b6310e5e85f1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:frac-ssm" data-paper-title="Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4881d67379b8f1c5">Why do multiple decay rates approximate a long tail better?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afrac-ssm">Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab, Montreal Research Center</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Log-spaced modes span recent and distant timescales, unlike a single exponential. Their finite combination approximates a bounded range, not infinite exact history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Fast modes track fluctuations while slow ones retain trends.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36314">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.36314-frac-ssm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4881d67379b8f1c5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:frac-ssm" data-paper-title="Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea7bf61d830b801b">What should finite-mode recurrence tests verify besides shape?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Afrac-ssm">Fractional State Space Transition for Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab, Montreal Research Center</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Verify equivalence to the finite-mode calculation, long-tail invariants, and state propagation. Operator checks are not reproduction of 1.3B training or model quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Inject an early impulse and compare combined decay over time with the defined approximation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36314">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2609.36314-frac-ssm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ea7bf61d830b801b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gated-attention" data-paper-title="Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-gated-attention-0685e39f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ec17b654ab0c8a26">Does the Gated Attention gate decide where to read or how much to emit?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agated-attention">Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Qwen / Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Attention first selects and aggregates positions. The current input then controls how much of each SDPA head output goes forward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A head can read a formatting marker but emit less when irrelevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2505.06708-gated-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ec17b654ab0c8a26">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gated-attention" data-paper-title="Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6609c4e775bab9c1">Why put the Gated Attention gate after SDPA rather than in logits?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agated-attention">Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Qwen / Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Aggregate each head first, then use an input-conditioned sigmoid before output projection. It controls how much of what was read is passed onward and adds nonlinearity between aggregation and projection. This is not changing historical softmax probabilities.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Suppress a head&#x27;s formatting output while retaining another head&#x27;s answer evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2505.06708-gated-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6609c4e775bab9c1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gated-attention" data-paper-title="Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-85ed640a6af63395">Why isn&#x27;t a pre-SDPA sigmoid equivalent to a post-SDPA gate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agated-attention">Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Qwen / Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Gating scores or values changes aggregation itself. The post-SDPA gate modulates the already aggregated output; placement is a documented ablation result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Scaling one contribution before combining differs from scaling the whole combined result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2505.06708-gated-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-85ed640a6af63395">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gated-attention" data-paper-title="Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5e263c96ab746d7a">Can a fixed constant replace a query-dependent per-head gate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agated-attention">Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Qwen / Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A constant loses input dependence and head selectivity. Produce sigmoid gates from current hidden state and multiply SDPA output before projection. Local gate statistics only verify a nontrivial path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Different questions over the same article can use different gates instead of always multiplying by 0.5.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2505.06708-gated-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5e263c96ab746d7a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gzip-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-gzip-sparse-attention-4236c23c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b01cb35887c2065a">Why compress raw byte blocks first?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agzip-sparse-attention">Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pennsylvania State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compression ratio is a training-free proxy for unique byte density and guides long-range edges, not a semantic importance label.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Repeated templates compress differently from unique IDs, but hard-to-compress gibberish can be useless.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.21752-gzip-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b01cb35887c2065a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gzip-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ff5a539f7aa258a3">Why give hard-to-gzip blocks long-range edges, and are they necessarily important?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agzip-sparse-attention">Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pennsylvania State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Blocks above the sample&#x27;s average compression-ratio threshold are treated as literal-rich and connected at range while preserving local windows and causality. Compressibility is a training-free proxy, not semantic gold; random noise can also be incompressible and too many literal blocks make edges costly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An unusual ID may need cross-section access while a repeated template compresses easily, but incompressible gibberish need not help.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.21752-gzip-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ff5a539f7aa258a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gzip-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-95f4b53dbe2b61f2">How does a gzip mask vary compared with a fixed BigBird or Longformer pattern?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agzip-sparse-attention">Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pennsylvania State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed masks use predetermined positions; gzip uses per-example block compressibility for literal edges and retains local windows. It avoids learned mask weights but pays for compression and construction, so edge counts do not establish speed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Moving a unique passage can move gzip edges without changing a positional pattern.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.21752-gzip-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-95f4b53dbe2b61f2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gzip-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-33a4f2c162cacc0b">Why intersect literal, local, and self edges with the causal mask?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agzip-sparse-attention">Parameter-free Adaptive Sparse Attention via Compression-Based Content Selection</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pennsylvania State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Their union expresses relevance, not chronology. Intersect it with causality and assign the appropriate masks to the three head types. Masking dense local scores does not accelerate a sparse kernel.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Selecting two literal blocks cannot let the early one read future tokens in the other.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.21752-gzip-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-33a4f2c162cacc0b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hymba" data-paper-title="Hymba: A Hybrid-head Architecture for Small Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-hymba-2cf1482a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0efbea46861fa34b">Why combine explicit historical reads and recurrent summaries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahymba">Hymba: A Hybrid-head Architecture for Small Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Attention directly retrieves positions, while the SSM compresses history into state. The same layer can use both without forcing either to carry every dependency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Explicit access can recover a name while recurrence carries grammar context.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13676">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2411.13676-hymba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0efbea46861fa34b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hymba" data-paper-title="Hymba: A Hybrid-head Architecture for Small Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-957edc876261c0c0">Why put attention and SSM in parallel within Hymba layers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahymba">Hymba: A Hybrid-head Architecture for Small Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The same input gets direct historical reads and a recurrent summary in one layer, then fuses both. This combines access mechanisms, not free compute; fusion, KV, and state budgets still matter.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One branch retrieves an old name while the other maintains running grammar state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13676">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2411.13676-hymba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-957edc876261c0c0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hymba" data-paper-title="Hymba: A Hybrid-head Architecture for Small Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c2fee06492c5f6c0">How does parallel Hymba differ from alternating attention and SSM layers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahymba">Hymba: A Hybrid-head Architecture for Small Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Parallel branches both read the same layer input and fuse in one update. Alternating layers transform the first branch&#x27;s result before the second computation. The graphs and fusion times differ at equal layer count.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two simultaneous readers share the original, unlike a second reader receiving only the first reader&#x27;s summary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13676">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2411.13676-hymba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c2fee06492c5f6c0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:hymba" data-paper-title="Hymba: A Hybrid-head Architecture for Small Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c7d03a30101239fb">Does the local Hymba path include all original features and throughput optimizations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Ahymba">Hymba: A Hybrid-head Architecture for Small Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · NVIDIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It fuses causal attention and a depthwise convolutional state branch, without meta tokens, 1.5B scale, or fused kernels. A runnable branch does not establish paper throughput.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Passing a small-model gated forward is a mechanism check, not a deployment speed measurement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13676">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2411.13676-hymba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c7d03a30101239fb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:kronlstm" data-paper-title="Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-kronlstm-ae88fcaa" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f0cf180efd09886f">What memory quantity does KronLSTM correct?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Akronlstm">Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johannes Kepler University Linz</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It corrects scalar association vᵀSk rather than forcing the entire retrieved vector to equal v. The update follows vkᵀ with separate forget and erase/write gates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Adjusting one association need not rewrite every value direction for that key.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26834">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.26834-kronlstm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f0cf180efd09886f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:kronlstm" data-paper-title="Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a233b49ed9960b21">Does KronLSTM update a full value vector or one scalar key–value association?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Akronlstm">Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johannes Kepler University Linz</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It uses vᵀSk and updates along vkᵀ, unlike correcting an entire vector error. Interference depends on overlap in both key and value; orthogonality on either side blocks that update&#x27;s interference. Forget, erase, and write are separate; do not multiply the write coefficient by the erase gate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Similar keys with orthogonal values do not interfere under one scalar association update, without guaranteeing no future interference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26834">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.26834-kronlstm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a233b49ed9960b21">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:kronlstm" data-paper-title="Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-949d6d4b470021a6">How does KronLSTM&#x27;s error differ from DeltaNet for interference analysis?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Akronlstm">Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johannes Kepler University Linz</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>DeltaNet uses Sk−v, while KronLSTM uses scalar vᵀSk−c. Interference involves both key and value inner products; one orthogonal side removes interference from this write, not all future forgetting.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Similar keys with orthogonal values can avoid interference despite key overlap.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26834">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.26834-kronlstm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-949d6d4b470021a6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:kronlstm" data-paper-title="Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b32ff25fb71361e2">Why not copy ordinary delta update&#x27;s forget direction and write coefficient?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Akronlstm">Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Johannes Kepler University Linz</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Forgetting acts on the right along the key axis. The decoupled write is c·vkᵀ, not βc·vkᵀ; only erase uses β. Compare an independent vec reference instead of checking loss alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Small β should not suppress the independent write gate c.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 实现与运行. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26834">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.26834-kronlstm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b32ff25fb71361e2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mamba" data-paper-title="Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-mamba-0b65990c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7a505778b7bd7571">Why does Mamba selectivity depend on the current token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amamba">Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University / Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Step size and read/write vectors depend on input, so retention, updates, and readout vary by content while still using recurrent state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A separator and answer token can trigger different updates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2312.00752-mamba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7a505778b7bd7571">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mamba" data-paper-title="Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-53597ba087ad9762">What does Mamba&#x27;s selectivity change inside the SSM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amamba">Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University / Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Token-dependent step sizes and read/write vectors control retention, write direction, and readout within recurrence. This is not output scaling of a fixed SSM. Linear sequence cost still does not guarantee exact arbitrary-token retrieval from finite state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Preserve state on filler but write differently for a key number; retrieval still depends on what remains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2312.00752-mamba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-53597ba087ad9762">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mamba" data-paper-title="Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7b1c8ad148c1bce8">How does Mamba memory differ from reweighting historical KV?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amamba">Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University / Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mamba accumulates history in state and uses input-dependent readout. Attention assigns weights directly to retained positions. Linear complexity does not imply lossless per-token history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A summary can retain a fact without separately addressable slots for every old word.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2312.00752-mamba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7b1c8ad148c1bce8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:mamba" data-paper-title="Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-275f57141b520ee1">Does a Python or PyTorch selective scan reproduce Mamba kernel throughput?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amamba">Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Carnegie Mellon University / Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A loop can check input-dependent parameters and recurrence, but not a fused parallel CUDA scan. The local run also omits 2.8B pretraining. Validate correctness, language quality, and throughput separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Seven steps agreeing with a reference check mechanics, not tokens per second.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2312.00752-mamba/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-275f57141b520ee1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-mosaics-plus" data-paper-title="Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-memory-mosaics-plus-a2cfe6c3" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6ed9deb0553b2192">Why evaluate test-time learning rather than IID performance alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-mosaics-plus">Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · FAIR, Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>IID testing does not show use of newly observed task experience. Mosaics+ combines recent dependence and long-term predictive associations to organize new-task evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use newly observed input/output examples to infer a rule rather than repeat old statistics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20782">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.20782-memory-mosaics-plus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6ed9deb0553b2192">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-mosaics-plus" data-paper-title="Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b087fe5457f11f79">Why normalize current and related-task memory separately in Mosaics+?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-mosaics-plus">Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · FAIR, Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One softmax lets numerous irrelevant past entries dilute current evidence. Two-stage retrieval normalizes each source then combines predictions. Short-term memory handles recent dependence, long-term stores predictive associations, and illegal future reads stay excluded.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Three relevant current entries should not be diluted solely because there are 1,000 old records.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20782">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.20782-memory-mosaics-plus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b087fe5457f11f79">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-mosaics-plus" data-paper-title="Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-68e8c0c69a84e1cc">How does two-stage Mosaics+ differ from a single softmax pool?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-mosaics-plus">Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · FAIR, Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate current and related-task normalization precedes combining. In a shared pool, adding even unrelated old entries can change current weight; these are different computations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Many old items should not drown out a few important current associations by count alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20782">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.20782-memory-mosaics-plus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-68e8c0c69a84e1cc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:memory-mosaics-plus" data-paper-title="Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-eff87d4df2d3102d">How does predictive value at i+1 avoid a future read?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amemory-mosaics-plus">Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · FAIR, Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Restrict i≤t−s with s≥1. Then i+1 is within the visible boundary. Split normalization at document boundaries and handle empty memory; reference loops and future perturbations are negative controls.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With skip=1, i=t−1 may use t but not t+1.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 结果与独立对照. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20782">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.20782-memory-mosaics-plus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eff87d4df2d3102d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:minimax-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="MiniMax Sparse Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-minimax-sparse-attention-fdb70645" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
