<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ttr-compressor" data-paper-title="Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-ttr-compressor-1230f560" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-453f6b16d07755e9">Does test-time compression retrain model parameters at inference?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Attr-compressor">Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It solves coefficients anew for each token group. Outer loss learns target projection and regularizer; closed-form per-input fitting does not update those parameters at inference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two inputs share a and ρ but solve different h.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31574v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.31574-ttr-compressor/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-453f6b16d07755e9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ttr-compressor" data-paper-title="Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0f87d6fafc5bcc63">Why normalize TTR keys but preserve target magnitudes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Attr-compressor">Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Unit keys group by direction; targets retain token strength. A static projection from the same normalized keys could be fit trivially and lose input-dependent compression. Per-forward coefficients do not update persistent parameters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Same-direction tokens of norm one and three have the same key but different targets; normalizing both would erase that distinction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31574v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.31574-ttr-compressor/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0f87d6fafc5bcc63">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ttr-compressor" data-paper-title="Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-9ee87e3a06c2bbc4">How does TTR differ from fixed mean pooling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Attr-compressor">Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It formulates and exactly solves a group-dependent ridge regression. Differentiating through the solve trains outer parameters; this is a different compression objective, not just new weights.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Groups with equal means but different directional correlations can yield different coefficients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31574v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.31574-ttr-compressor/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9ee87e3a06c2bbc4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:ttr-compressor" data-paper-title="Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-70dfe34e2a284c5f">Why solve a T×T token-space system, and why not detach?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Attr-compressor">Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Chinese University of Hong Kong</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Scale K by D inverse square root, solve I_T plus the scaled K Gram matrix by Cholesky, then map to d dimensions. The outer loss needs solve gradients for projection and regularization. Complexity retains a cubic T term.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Token-space is attractive when T≪d but is not always only O(T²d).</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31574v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.31574-ttr-compressor/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-70dfe34e2a284c5f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:select-ttt" data-paper-title="Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-select-ttt-1dc0ac0a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-99cdb22b8325ac12">Does Select-TTT change retrieval or the strength of writes to fast weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aselect-ttt">Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It keeps In-Place TTT chunk writes and scales each chunk&#x27;s learning rate with question relevance. Scores come from question-token negative log probabilities under the frozen LM head. It neither trains a retriever nor discards all low-scoring chunks. Different questions can induce different multipliers.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A long conversation may favor different passages for a moving date and food preferences, without labels telling the model where the answer is.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36794v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36794-select-ttt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-99cdb22b8325ac12">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:select-ttt" data-paper-title="Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0936a469597e97bb">Why average the lowest-CE positions in a chunk rather than the highest?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aselect-ttt">Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>CE is mean negative log probability of question tokens under the current hidden state&#x27;s vocabulary distribution. Lower values mean the position predicts question words better. Averaging the lowest k preserves local relevance more robustly than a single minimum. Reversing it reinforces irrelevant positions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: For CE 1 and 6, select 1 as more relevant. Repeated question tokens count as many times as they appear.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36794v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36794-select-ttt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0936a469597e97bb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:select-ttt" data-paper-title="Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-aa77181e9a488912">Why isn&#x27;t Select-TTT a strictly conserved write-budget allocation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aselect-ttt">Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Softmax multiplied by chunk count sums to that count before clipping. An upper cap can lower the sum. Approximate mean learning-rate preservation is not strict conservation. Renormalization changes Eq. 10 and can violate the per-chunk cap.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Three chunks can start near [3,0,0]. A cap of 1.2 gives total about 1.2, not 3; this is a formula example, not a QA result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36794v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36794-select-ttt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aa77181e9a488912">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:select-ttt" data-paper-title="Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f70c34eaf358e479">Why emit the current chunk before writing its keys and values?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aselect-ttt">Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · University of Science and Technology of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Its outputs read the pre-update state; only later chunks use the new information. Writing first leaks the current update into an earlier output and changes causal order. The local reference tests tensor-state transitions, not real NTP-aligned features, backbone integration or long-dialogue evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Start with W=0. Chunk one outputs 0 then writes W=1. Chunk two can read 1; an output of 1 in chunk one would use its write prematurely.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36794v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36794-select-ttt/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f70c34eaf358e479">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:sleep-lti" data-paper-title="Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-sleep-lti-911eb3e3" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d2752590c7dbcbcf">Is Sleep just a pause or a separate learning stage?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asleep-lti">Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It is offline consolidation. Before applying precomputed base updates, expand slow modules and use the pre-update teacher to consolidate fast memories into the student to be updated. Then apply the update and clear sending-layer experts. It is not just a pause or brief replay, and the full chain is not implemented locally.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Verify notes copied into a long-term library before deleting the temporary notes. Computing note similarity is not consolidation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 高成本完整实验. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03979v2">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2606.03979-sleep-lti/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d2752590c7dbcbcf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:sleep-lti" data-paper-title="Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-357fc7df50a38180">Does LTI&#x27;s edit-distance threshold cap edit count or a similarity ratio?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asleep-lti">Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It caps the absolute number of token edits, inclusively. For accepted pairs the literal reward is one minus distance divided by the longer completion length. A fixed similarity-ratio threshold differs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Threshold 1 admits one substitution in both 6- and 60-token completions, with rewards 5/6 and 59/60.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03979v2">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2606.03979-sleep-lti/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-357fc7df50a38180">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:sleep-lti" data-paper-title="Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7ed013edbf092629">Does crossing the literal-distance threshold also zero semantic reward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asleep-lti">Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A separate frozen judge assigns binary semantic reward. The threshold only gates the literal branch. Very different wording can preserve meaning; replacing the judge with edit distance changes the method.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: With gamma 0.4 and a positive semantic judgment, a zero literal branch still yields total reward 0.4.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03979v2">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2606.03979-sleep-lti/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7ed013edbf092629">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:sleep-lti" data-paper-title="Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-da8dd16e738119ab">Can the local Sleep reward prove the model retains knowledge long term?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asleep-lti">Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It receives tokenized completions and external semantic labels and checks reward boundaries. No dream sampling, CMS, expansion, LoRA, screening or forgetting evaluation. The costly full experiment is not reproduced; the kernel is not an Evolve capability operator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Reward 0.9 for two integer sequences confirms the formula for that input, not any update to model weights.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现与边界, 高成本完整实验. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03979v2">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2606.03979-sleep-lti/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-da8dd16e738119ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:merlin" data-paper-title="Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-merlin-4afaa9c4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8c1c0aafb3dafdad">Why can two key segments with the same mean require different attention routing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amerlin">Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mean alignment can hide strong key matches canceled by others. MERLIN also retains raw second moments and recovers query-direction alignment variance, mixing it with mean routing. It enriches segment routing without reconstructing full per-token attention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keys [-2,2] and [0,0] both average zero. Query 1 gives alignment variances 4 and 0, invisible to mean routing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37645v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.37645-merlin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8c1c0aafb3dafdad">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:merlin" data-paper-title="Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-e291827c8e0288f6">Why does Eq. 7 distinguish the second moment from covariance?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amerlin">Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It stores mean(kkᵀ), without centering, then computes variance qᵀΣq−(qᵀμ)². Passing covariance and subtracting again double-centers; treating the raw moment as variance includes mean strength. The local reference directly measures dot-product variance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keys [1,3] have mean 2, moment 5 and variance 1. Using 5 overcounts by 4; subtracting 4 from centered 1 yields the invalid −3.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37645v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.37645-merlin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e291827c8e0288f6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:merlin" data-paper-title="Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6a6cbfe669675cd8">Why not mix logits then apply one softmax instead of mixing two softmax distributions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amerlin">Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Softmax is nonlinear. MERLIN normalizes mean and variance routes separately and mixes probabilities with gamma. Mixing logits first changes competition and normalization even though both outputs sum to one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Mean logits [4,0], variance logits [0,0], gamma 0.5 yield [0.741,0.259]; softmax of mixed logits [2,0] gives [0.881,0.119].</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37645v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.37645-merlin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6a6cbfe669675cd8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:merlin" data-paper-title="Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d276140dff602bb">Why only expose completed segments to local queries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Amerlin">Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Princeton University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Full-segment means and moments include future tokens for queries inside that segment. A full model could maintain prefix moments and recurrent state; the local path does not. It exposes completed segments only and rejects calls with none visible, rather than leaking future statistics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Segment start 4 length 4 covers positions 4–7. It is not visible at 6, only at 7; reading all keys at 4 leaks positions 5–7.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37645v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.37645-merlin/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d276140dff602bb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:semantic-block-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-semantic-block-sparse-attention-d240ec17" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-71133fb6ad7e7dfb">Why does Coarse Semantic Blocks not simply group consecutive tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asemantic-block-sparse-attention">Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · Preferred Networks</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It clusters normalized keys, allowing distant positions to share a block. Neighboring positions share a window but need not express similar information. A centroid score retrieves several related positions at once. Large blocks can also include irrelevant tokens, so cheaper routing does not guarantee unchanged retrieval quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: Early and late passages both discuss temperature, so their keys may share a block while intervening person-related tokens belong elsewhere. This explains indexing, not a RULER result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04313">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.04313-semantic-block-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-71133fb6ad7e7dfb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:semantic-block-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4b6efe762227b2d8">Why apply centroid softmax in each query head before GQA summation and the size penalty?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asemantic-block-sparse-attention">Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · Preferred Networks</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each head first produces its own block-preference distribution. Summing within the GQA group combines preferences, then dividing by visible block size penalizes expensive blocks. Summing logits before softmax changes the nonlinear order and can let one head&#x27;s strong negative score cancel another head&#x27;s support.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: Two heads strongly favor A and B respectively. Summing their distributions preserves both preferences; averaging logits first can create an uninformative tie. If A has eight visible tokens and B two, their size penalties must also differ.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 实现与运行. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04313">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.04313-semantic-block-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4b6efe762227b2d8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:semantic-block-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-cd74fc8a1e3d6afc">Why not use centroids or normalized keys directly for attention after routing?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asemantic-block-sparse-attention">Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · Preferred Networks</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Normalized spherical vectors only select support. Final attention still uses original QKV and scaled dot products. Replacing member values with centroids discards token content, while normalizing attention keys changes magnitude sensitivity. The full-budget dense limit checks this boundary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: Two parallel keys have norms one and ten, so routing may cluster them together. Original attention can still prefer the norm-ten token. Normalizing both for attention erases that distinction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04313">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.04313-semantic-block-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cd74fc8a1e3d6afc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:semantic-block-sparse-attention" data-paper-title="Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a5d81bbbe5d186d">Why can K=1 retrieve three history tokens, and what does the causal mask actually establish?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Asemantic-block-sparse-attention">Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · Preferred Networks</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Selection accumulates whole blocks until reaching or exceeding K, allowing last-block overshoot. Truncating a block changes the method. The mask only prevents attention from reading future positions; fitting centroids on the entire prompt can still depend on future keys. Unindexed generated tokens must stay in the unconditional region.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: If the highest-scoring block has three history tokens, K=1 still retrieves all three plus the current token. Changing future keys and refitting can change an early selection, so zero future support does not establish absence of every future influence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 检查与负控, 成本判断与复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04313">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.04313-semantic-block-sparse-attention/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1a5d81bbbe5d186d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:anchor-kv" data-paper-title="Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-anchor-kv-2d58f519" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-98ae0a3c522d4faa">If Anchor finds cross-layer state redundancy, why not let every layer read the same matrix directly?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aanchor-kv">Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · University of Arizona</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Related content does not imply identical coordinate bases. Each reader needs a learned linear map to express shared information in its own basis; the writer retains its basis. Copying a state without a map confuses shared content with compatible coordinates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: One layer writes a direction as (1,0), while another layer&#x27;s basis represents it as (0,1). Shared content is unchanged, but a reader rotation is needed to recover the intended direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04327">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.04327-anchor-kv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-98ae0a3c522d4faa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:anchor-kv" data-paper-title="Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6287dfe38707de43">What problem does the input-dependent gate solve in Anchor&#x27;s shared readout?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aanchor-kv">Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · University of Arizona</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The gate controls how much long-range readout each head adds to local output. It can suppress noisy memory on short-window tasks and admit memory when distant information matters. It is a trainable sigmoid projection, not a fixed one-half coefficient or an arbitrary reranker after concatenation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: With local output two and memory ten, a near-zero gate gives approximately two; gate .2 gives four. This is an additive-gating calculation, not task accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04327">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.04327-anchor-kv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6287dfe38707de43">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:anchor-kv" data-paper-title="Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8944d4335eeacb8a">Why does Anchor&#x27;s deployment state reduction not justify removing interior branches at the start of training?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aanchor-kv">Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · University of Arizona</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The paper retains interior TTT in both training stages to stabilize gradients and removes it only for deployment. Inference memory savings do not show that training without those branches converges or that all layer states were identical. The local read-map component does not certify the full recipe.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: Training retains several gradient entry points and deployment keeps shared ones, like removing scaffolding after construction. The completed building&#x27;s lack of scaffolding does not show construction never needed it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 成本判断与复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04327">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2611.04327-anchor-kv/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8944d4335eeacb8a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:anchor-kv" data-paper-title="Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="foundation-models" data-topic="foundation-models/context-and-state">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Foundation models / Long context: attention, recurrent state, and memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1ac32bc7c0c54bdc">Why does the local external-writer interface not establish an implemented LaCT/Muon TTT update?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aanchor-kv">Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-04 · University of Arizona</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It only accepts externally computed state, validates the designated writer and increasing revision, and lets readers learn maps and gates. LaCT&#x27;s inner objective, momentum/Muon and model installation remain outside scope. An arbitrary SGD step or fixed matrix cannot stand in for complete Anchor acceptance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: Writing an observed KV matrix at revision one checks shared reading. A reader attempting revision two must be rejected. Correct interface behavior still does not establish useful TTT training in a 7B model.</p>

<details class="ar-learning-guide" markdown="1"><summary>Topic guide and reading order</summary>

## Start with this question

As context grows, does the model preserve addressable historical tokens or a compressed recurrent state?

## Takeaway

Separate position, information access, and state capacity. RoPE rotates two-dimensional Q/K subspaces by position so dot products capture relative offsets; attention still accesses history within its window. Mamba makes state-update steps and read/write parameters input-dependent and compresses history into recurrent state. Sparse and hybrid attention lie between these approaches, reading selected history or retaining full access in some layers. MERLIN aggregates reads across state segments: routing-key first and second moments recover query-aligned means and variances, then separate softmaxes are mixed through a gate. This is not Mamba's state recurrence.

## Example

Suppose a document defines x at the start and asks for it 30,000 tokens later. Full attention can address the location; a recurrent model must keep the relevant information in state. With a local window, check for global layers or extra memory rather than trusting a context-length claim alone.

## Common pitfall

Linear complexity does not guarantee exact long-distance retrieval or real hardware speed. RoPE does not guarantee unlimited extrapolation. Check state, window, training length, and position scaling together. Local small-model results are not paper-scale evidence.

## Reading order

Start with RoFormer's Q/K rotations, then Mamba's input-dependent state updates. Compare directly reading history with encoding history in state before moving to sparse attention, hybrids, or external memory.

1. [RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding](../../../../reproductions/2104.09864-rope/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864)
2. [Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces](../../../../reproductions/2312.00752-mamba/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752)

## Check your understanding

If two models accept 32k inputs, can they recover arbitrary details from the first segment equally well?

??? note "Show suggested answer"

    No. Input length describes the interface or operating range. Direct addressing, window clipping, state capacity, and training distributions differ. Test retrieval with controlled positions and distractor lengths under the same budget.
